utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric, case number IT-03-68-T.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in a language you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can follow the proceedings in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution team, together with co-counsels, Ms. Patricia Sellers and Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and our case manager Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wubben. Good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Vasvija Vidovic, together with Mr. John Jones, representing Mr. Naser Oric. And we have our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, with us, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic. And good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries before we go straight to business? MR. DI FAZIO: I just wonder if Your Honours could indicate the order of business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, that's very easy. I intended to start with last point that arose yesterday, and that's the matter of why that document was -- you say it was disclosed together with hundreds of other documents. MR. DI FAZIO: I'd be glad to address you on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. While the Defence maintains that that document was not disclosed properly as one of the documents relating to a witness that you intended to bring forward. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know if it would assist Your Honour at this point, but we'd prepared a brief chronology relating to that statement and attached correspondence which we can pass up to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that would be useful. Before we go ahead, just let me alert you to something. I was informed this morning by my staff here, by our staff here, that there is a technical problem today, namely, that the delay transmission apparatus is not working properly, and that basically that means we had to choose either to sit in private session or closed session, which none of us would like to do, or else risk it and go live as we are actually doing. This entails on each and every one of us an extra burden, and this is that we need to pay more attention than usual not to mention names that we usually would easily redact without consequences, because this time there is no possibility of redacting in an effective manner, because the transmission would have already gone on air. So I appeal to you to be extra careful in mentioning names of possible protected witnesses. I don't know if we have any this morning. I doubt it. But one needs to be extra careful, please. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, if I could just pass up -- pass up that bundle, I think it might be of assistance. I don't know if it also might assist for me, perhaps, to go first and outline what precisely our objections were, before Mr. Di Fazio responds. It's a matter for Your Honours, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were you given a copy of this before, Mr. Di Fazio, or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm providing it now. MR. DI FAZIO: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I'll give you two minutes, three minutes to go through it before you say what you have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Should I explain the chronology, if that would be useful. If I might say, our point yesterday is, of course, not that we never received --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise. If you give my learned friend the opportunity to read through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I said. I said I'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Then it's perhaps better not to start right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones, I mean, let Mr. Di Fazio -- give Mr. Di Fazio the opportunity to read -- time to read this. MR. DI FAZIO: I think I get the gist of it, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, are you ready? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. The only explanation I want is this: From what I gather, that at a certain point in time, it appears, at least from the 3rd or 4th March of this year onwards, you should have been aware of the existence of this second statement of Svetlana Trifunovic. It's true, there's no question about it, that you made the documents, the rules of the road documents relating to the Naser Oric file, available for inspection, and that inspection, in fact, took place. There's no question about it. But in making those documents available for inspection, and they being inspected is one thing. Handing even -- even handing them over is another thing. But disclosure under Rule 66 for the purpose of that particular rule in relation to a witness that you intend to bring forward is another matter. That is a completely separate and distinct kind of disclosure. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know it can be argued that you had nothing to hide, because if you made it available for inspection, you definitely had -- were not attempting to hide it from the Defence. But that's not the point. MR. DI FAZIO: The Defence examined, as you say, inspected, various rules of the road materials on the 19th, 20th, and 21st of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Over a three-day period. On the 28th of July, the Defence wrote to the Prosecution, seeking a large number of documents that had been the result of their inspection, a large number of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 28th? MR. DI FAZIO: 28th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 2-8? MR. DI FAZIO: 28th of July. They headed the letter "disclosure of the Oric case following inspections at the OTP."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was this in writing? Because We don't have a copy of it. MR. DI FAZIO: It's in writing. I don't know if it's in the bundle handed up to you by Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I don't see it. After the 28th of July, the next document dates 2nd August 2004. Yes, go ahead. MR. DI FAZIO: After the 28th of July, the Defence wrote to us and sought all sorts of documents that they listed in annexes attached to the letter, including one particular annex, annex 3, which they headed "documents from the Rule 66(B) file pursuant to inspection dated 19th of July 2004. Note to OTP: Please provide us with copies of all the documents which we have marked with a VV in the right margin. Where we have written complete doc, comp doc, whole doc, or document in full, then please provide us with the whole document. Note the use of dittos; for example, in the case of documents relating to a certain person, we are asking for whole documents in all cases." And then very helpfully, the Defence proceeded to list the names of various persons, many of whom are witnesses in -- or were witnesses as part of the Prosecution case. It's a long, lengthy document, and provides very detailed instructions from the Defence -- well, requests from the Defence to the Prosecution, specifying the particular documents. You go through them, and eventually it has all sorts of notations on it, in handwriting as well, and eventually you get to Svetlana Trifunovic, and they ask for document RR321758, and they ask for the whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the reference? MR. DI FAZIO: RR321758.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we have the document from yesterday? Madam Registrar, this was D81.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honours, if it helps, on the front of the chronology, we have the RR number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what I want --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, the document being referred to by my friend is in the bundle where you have Svetlana Trifunovic. Our point is we never receive it until the 27th of September, not that we didn't request it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if you received it, then you received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There's never been any dispute that we received it. It's a question of the Rule 66(A)(ii) disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I assume that if you asked specifically for a document relating to Svetlana Trifunovic, you knew that Svetlana Trifunovic was a prospective witness, because in a previous document - as number 21 - you had indicated her name as being witness number 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I would expect what's good for the goose is good for the gander, and if I am to expect diligence on the part of the Prosecution, equally I am to expect diligence on the part of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Absolutely. We've been pursuing these documents and the others, many of which we haven't received disclosure of to this date. You'll see in this bundle, Your Honour, there's a 66(A)(ii) receipt which is what we typically receive from the Prosecution when they disclose a prior statement. There is no such receipt for Svetlana Trifunovic, and we did only receive the document in four boxes of material on the 27th of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the RR number is not the same. You said, Mr. Di Fazio, 372518. This document that we had yesterday is 321946. It's not because I want to be finicky, but I think these --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's within the range. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But it's not the same document. What I mean to say, it's not the same document. MR. DI FAZIO: But it's within that range of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But in other words, what Mr. Jones or Madam Vidovic, or whoever, asked you to provide in relation to Ms. Svetlana Trifunovic was not this document, it's another document. MR. DI FAZIO: It was included in a range of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the range that you have then with regard to -- MR. DI FAZIO: 321758, 322261.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see, uh-huh. Continuous, in other words. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, yes. It's within that bundle of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Then that solves it, okay. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, it's within that bundle of documents. My apologies. If I can assist, the numbers are RR321758, RR322261. And I apologise for speaking so fast. If Your Honours please, the point the Prosecution wanted to make has been made already. It's a simple point. This was a focused and specific request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely. MR. DI FAZIO: It was a focused and specific request on the part of the Defence that was replied to and accommodated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that doesn't change something which is fundamental, Mr. Di Fazio, that it shouldn't be that the Defence asks the Prosecution to provide it with a particular document relating to a particular witness. It is exactly the opposite, the other way around. It should be the Prosecution, once it identifies that document as relating to a witness, as being a statement of a witness that you intend to bring forward, to disclose it immediately to the Defence. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I appreciate that, Your Honour, and I don't shrink from that. And yes, it would have been desirable to hand it over sooner. It would have been. But disclosure continues in this case, it's ongoing as we speak, and it will not stop --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we're talking about March 2004. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not talking of a week ago or two weeks ago or one month ago when we started the trial. We're talking of a good nine months ago, basically, eight months ago. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You had them, presumably, all these documents, between the 3rd and the 4th of March. I grant you, you needed a whole month to catalogue them, to see where each document -- to which pigeon hole it belonged, whether it belonged to particular witnesses. I grant you that. I grant you two months. But we're talking now of September, when you finally end. You gave the impression yesterday, at least, that you came here yesterday with the firm doubt in your mind that it could well be that the Defence were not even aware of the existence of this document. MR. DI FAZIO: If I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I cannot allow a situation like that. MR. DI FAZIO: If I gave that impression, then it's not the impression that I sought to convey to Your Honour yesterday. Something was said to me yesterday before court started that made me doubt my clear and firm understanding that I had been informed that that particular document, the document that was used in cross-examination yesterday, might not have been disclosed. And that is what caused me -- caused my immediate alarm, because I had made specific inquiries in relation to that document, and I'd been satisfied that it had been disclosed. So yesterday a comment was made to me that made me doubt my clear and firm understanding. Accordingly, I walked the distance from here to the Defence table to ensure that that -- what I hoped was not the case was, in fact, not the case, and Mr. Jones confirmed that. That's the impression that I wanted to convey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No one is attributing bad faith to you or to your colleagues, Mr. Di Fazio. Please don't read me wrong. But this is not the way things should go, should happen. I mean, it's simply -- well, I expect this disclosure, particularly in a case which is not a big case -- this is not a big case, this is a fairly small case, with a fairly small number of witnesses, certainly not with a small amount of documents, I acknowledge that. But to tell me that until the day when the witness is about to give evidence, one has sufficient space to harbour doubts as to whether disclosure has been made properly, as it should, or indirectly because it just happened to happen, it's not fair. It's not done. MR. DI FAZIO: I appreciate that, and I don't try to shrink from that, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I don't want to make a mountain out of a mole hill, because there's no damage done, basically. MR. DI FAZIO: That is -- I have to make that point, and I know that Your Honour, I know that Your Honour may not want to hear that point, but I must press that point. Yes, you are right, Your Honour is right that it should have been a direct -- it should have been in a letter, saying, here is the previous statement of that witness given to the Serb authorities years ago. That is correct, and I don't shrink from that. That would have been the desirable course, if Your Honours please. But had the events having occurred in the way they did, the Defence has suffered no prejudice at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I acknowledge as well. I acknowledge as well. But it is not -- when these things happen, certainly they are not conducive to the environment that I tried to secure from the beginning, from the very first day of this trial, because at that point in time, I would never blame -- I was a defence lawyer myself before I became a judge, okay, because I come from a system where, like in the United Kingdom, you're selected from the bar. And I don't mean from a place where you drink, I mean from a place where you exercise the profession. And I know that when such things happen, suspicion creeps in. And the last thing I want in this case is to have it flounder on the basis of defective disclosure or anything like that. Let it go either way, this way or that way. None of us really cares. I mean, we just want to make sure that justice prevails. But let's not have a case which becomes a mistrial or flounders precisely because of defective disclosure or non-disclosure. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I understand that. I have absolutely no quarrels with what Your Honour has said. Your Honour is, of course, absolutely correct. But if you look at the way the events unfolded yesterday, and if you look at the content of the motions that have been put in by the Defence relating to the issue of disclosure, this is not one of their complaints. This is not one of their complaints --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it -- MR. DI FAZIO: It became a complaint yesterday, if Your Honours please, because as a matter of courtesy, I wanted to satisfy myself that my understanding had, in fact, been correct, and so I approached the Defence to make sure that I hadn't made a mistake and that the document had been disclosed. The result is a complaint about disclosure. But up until that moment, there had been, as far as I understand, I don't think that document is the subject of any of the motions. I'm sure Mr. Jones will correct me if I'm wrong. But it hadn't been the subject of any specific complaint. It became a complaint following my approach to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It had to become a complaint, Mr. Di Fazio. What do you expect? I mean, you had Mr. Jones who said, I quote his own words, "This document came to light not because it was pointed out to us specifically by the Prosecution but as a result of the diligence of the Defence team." I mean, step number 2 is very obvious. This document should have been disclosed under Rule 66, and it wasn't disclosed. Step number 3, whatever you say, there's always going to be a complaint about non-disclosure. I mean, it's unavoidable. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, with respect, of course, it was disclosed, but it was disclosed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was not disclosed under Rule 66 as a document relating to a prospective witness. MR. DI FAZIO: My understanding, if Your Honours please, is that it was disclosed on the 27th of September, 2004, at the very latest. If Mr. Jones has any quarrel with that issue, perhaps he could let us know if that is so. And it was disclosed by way of a letter dated the 27th of September, 2004, to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We should see that letter, if Mr. Di Fazio is going to put forward that that letter specifically refers to prior statement of Svetlana Trifunovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely he's not going to refer to that, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There's no quibble.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not waste time. However, do you want to take the floor on this, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very shortly, because I intent to bring this argument to a close.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I would simply make four brief points in reply. Firstly, this is the second time this has happened. During the testimony of Dr. Fagel, Mr. Di Fazio provided me with a document during the break, again, a very important document that we'll see today, and so as Your Honours says, you know, once bitten, twice shy, although those weren't Your Honour's words. Secondly, I do want to make clear for the record that this document is from the rules of the road file, which means it was provided by the Serb authorities to the Tribunal in this case. And I mention that as an aside simply because Your Honour Judge Eser was referring to Latin and Cyrillic scripts. This is a document provided by the Serbs to this Tribunal. So I just wanted that to be clear for the record. But I just did want to clarify, my objection to the OTP's conduct was twofold. It wasn't that we hadn't received the document. Obviously, we received it. We had to do some fairly fancy footwork to make sure that the registrar had it with him in translation in Belgrade. But that's another matter. But my point was really this, and I'd like to just pass up the proofing notes for Ms. Trifunovic so that Your Honours can follow me on this point. And it's that her evidence appeared to be certainly that the document was shown to her. That document was taken to Belgrade by Mr. Di Fazio, so he obviously considered it an important document. It was shown to her, and her evidence appeared to be that she even signed it. Now, you'll see from the highlighted section on the second page that essentially Ms. Trifunovic adopted the statement in the sense that, in the proofing notes, she made one or two corrections. She said, well, this appears to be a mistake, it wasn't my aunt's house, it was my house, I don't recall a wounded man. But she implies the rest of the statement was all right, that she was basically adopting that as her statement. And in that context, I consider it inappropriate for Mr. Di Fazio to seek to suggest in re-examination that this was a mere piece of paper which didn't have any probative value, when he knew full well from proofing her that she had essentially adopted this statement, and maybe even signed it. Now, our experience in this case, and Your Honours may have a similar experience, is that often when a witness is shown a document, that they're then asked to sign it. Now, Mr. Di Fazio, who's said that he didn't ask her to sign the document, and so we can't take that matter any further. But obviously if it had been signed by her, then one has a new document, and I was suggesting that that document should have been disclosed to us. But we can leave that to one side. Then there is the matter that it wasn't disclosed to us clearly as a prior statement, under Rule 66(A)(ii) which may seem academic, but it isn't, because it does show a breakdown in the Prosecution's system of disclosure, particularly even with regard to Rule 68. And this is a statement dated the 5th of February, 1993, when the witness was giving evidence that she was in custody until the 18th of February, 1993. She says in that statement that she was only detained for two days as opposed to a month. It's clearly a Rule 68 statement as well and should have been disclosed to us for that reason. As I said, I don't wish to dwell on this. We can come back to some of these matters perhaps over the motions in the afternoon. But I would point out that in the bundle with the chronology which Your Honour has, where there is a list of documents with the initials next to it, which we have asked for that we still have not received, most of those documents, including for Slavoljub Filipovic, who will be giving evidence next week. And indeed there are documents relating to witnesses who have testified already; Stanisa Stevanovic, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is not a protected witness, I hope?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. And as Your Honour points out, there is clearly a separate obligation under Rule 66 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely. I mean, especially -- this becomes a very important matter, because as the rules have been changed, and probably will continue to change, to facilitate the disclosure process that the Prosecution is burdened with; on the other hand, or simultaneously, the rights -- the specific rights of disclosure under 66 and 68 have to be applied with more rigour. It is so obvious. It is no excuse to say, Now we have a system whereby all our archives are available and come, please, and sit down and you can see whatever you like. That's not disclosure. It is a kind of disclosure, but it is not the disclosure that is required, the particular disclosure that's required under 66 and 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I would end only by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would agree, Your Honour, and I would end by simply requesting that the Prosecution review this correspondence again, particularly for witnesses who are going to be testifying, as well as for those who have testified, and provide us with the materials we've requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the other hand, unless my colleagues would like to raise anything in this regard, I honestly think that we should bring this matter to an end. I think there is agreement amongst us that no damage, no prejudice has been caused, because sort of -- it was a kind of an automatic remedy to the unfortunate occurrence. I don't think that we're talking of a prejudice anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you give this back to Mr. Jones, please. Thank you. The thing is this: The worst part of it, as I see it, is that when these incidents arise, they are time-consuming. We have already lost practically an hour between yesterday and today. That's an hour gone. And I think the money and the resources of this Tribunal can be used to much better purposes. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio, please try to be as brief as possible so that we close this. MR. DI FAZIO: I've got nothing further to say on this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. About the next witness, that one of next week? MR. DI FAZIO: It's about Your Honours, I understood, wanted to conduct a -- hear submissions on two recent motions provided --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I apologise. But in the last part of his submission Mr. Jones mentioned a particular witness who is supposed to be coming forward next week to give evidence, and that also in that case, you have failed to furnish the Defence with -- what is, exactly, the position, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm referring, if you look again at the bundle with the chronology at the front, within that, you have these indices with ERN numbers and initials VV, whole doc, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then you'll find there Filipovic on page -- I'm sorry, the pages aren't numbered, but you'll see his name there. And you will see that we have requested --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slavoljub?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. We have requested a lot of documents relating to that witness, and we haven't received all of those documents. If I confer with my colleague, I can see how much, if anything, we have received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps this you could sort out amongst yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have received nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have received nothing? Why is that? MR. DI FAZIO: I haven't prepared for Slavoljub -- I haven't looked into that, if Your Honours please, and I can answer you without going back, spending time looking at the correspondence and looking at the issue. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the case manager, can the case manager find out whether -- because this goes back to -- MR. DI FAZIO: She's apparently doing it now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because there are the ERN numbers, and I -- from -- at least from what I know is that your record would show when that document was disclosed. MR. DI FAZIO: It should. It should. It should. But that needs time, to look at the correspondence and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can give her -- usher, please, you can give the case manager this document here. This is the gentleman we're talking about, Filipovic, Slavoljub. And she can check while you talk, or while we discuss this. MR. DI FAZIO: If that can be achieved now, we'll do that for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: But what I wanted to raise with you, it's not the earlier issue, it's this: One of the motions that was due for discussion today concerns the non-disclosure of a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I wonder if you want to deal with that now, because I can be very brief there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we're talking of the first supplement to Defence Rule 68 motion; is that correct? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The one filed on the 18th of November. MR. DI FAZIO: We are. We are. And it strikes me as an appropriate time to deal with that, given --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have -- do you have any objection, Judge Brydensholt, to deal with that? No? We can deal with it. However, before you start, before I give you the floor, Mr. Di Fazio, because I think the public ought to know what we're talking about. I mean, because you and us and the Defence know exactly what we're talking about. But members of the public in the gallery, or on the other side, who are following this -- the transmissions, wouldn't even know what we're talking about. On the 10th of September, 2004, there was a Defence motion filed requesting an order for measures to ensure that the Prosecution complies with Rule 68. Rule 68 deals, inter alia, with disclosure of exculpatory material or material that could shed light on the credibility of witnesses; inter alia, I say. At the time, this was at a time prior to the commencement of this trial, we debated this motion briefly. However, this motion was not ruled upon. And more or less, we entrusted ourselves in your hands, particularly in the hands of the Prosecution, making it clear that any serious failure to disclose pursuant to -- material pursuant to Rule 68 would be taken very, very seriously. Then subsequently, on the 18th of November, another motion was filed by the Defence, and this is called the first supplement to Defence Rule 68 motion. The supplement to this motion details general problems with Rule 68 disclosures that, according to the Defence, are being encountered in this case, and also gives one example. Before I proceed any further, I want to make sure that the person mentioned, the Croat mentioned in the motion, is not a protected witness. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm not aware of any protective requirements, and in any event, he's not a witness in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. The Defence refers to a statement made by a certain Andjelko Makar, a Croat, who allegedly held high-ranking positions in the TO and subsequently in the 2nd Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in a period which is relevant to the indictment. This statement allegedly was taken by -- from that person by an OTP investigator, Mr. Nasir. According to the Defence, the statement was not disclose indeed a timely manner, but almost eight months after it was taken. Furthermore, it was not disclosed pursuant to Rule 68 but under Rule 66(B). According to the Defence, the statement includes portions which are clearly exculpatory, and instances are given in the supplementary motion. This is basically it, except that the Defence also points out that in the event of late Rule 68 disclosures, the Prosecution tends to focus on whether this has caused the Defence any prejudice or not, although this is not one of the requirements for disclosure under Rule 68, rather than addressing the issues causing delayed disclosure. The Defence also stresses that in the case of the individual I mentioned earlier, Makar, there has been prejudice since it contains information which the Defence would have liked to pass on to its military expert in a timely manner and well before the Prosecution military expert testifies. Finally, the Defence requests the Trial Chamber to take appropriate measures to ensure that these instances to precipatorial non-compliance with Rule 68 do not recur, including an order to the Prosecution to report on the steps it is taking to address its repeated failures promptly to disclose exculpatory material to the Defence. So this much not because any of us needed to know this, but because otherwise we would have had a discussion which, for all intents and purposes to outsiders, would have been above their heads and would have not been able to follow properly. That is not the purpose of the element of publicity under which the trials should take place. Yes. Now, Mr. Di Fazio, I saw you were very anxious to address this supplementary motion. And thank God this is Friday, because usually I'm more aggressive on a Monday. MR. DI FAZIO: I wouldn't say anxious, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. MR. DI FAZIO: I think I can cut out 50 per cent of the work that the Defence needs to do on this motion, because I -- the Prosecution is going to make certain concessions in regard to this particular document. The Prosecution concedes that there has been late disclosure of this document. The period of time between its taking in March and its disclosure was far too long, and cannot be defended in any temporal sense. The periods of time is just too long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who is responsible? MR. DI FAZIO: I'll try to get to that point, if I can, Your Honours, as best I can. As best I can. And the second issue that I want to concede on is that it does contain Rule 68 material. Whereas undoubtedly it was also disclosable under Rule 66(B), it clearly contained Rule 68 material, in the Prosecution's view. So what you have here is a situation where disclosure has occurred, but it's not occurred within the full ambit of the rule, which requires disclosure as soon as practicable. And that's not happened. So in that sense, if that is a breach of Rule 68, then there has been a breach of Rule 68, although now it's been rectified in the sense that the statement has been handed over. The focus of the previous motion by the Defence concerning their generalised complaints about disclosure of the Prosecution and this motion is that they suppose that there is a systematic problem with the Prosecution, because there are, they say, instances where material has -- which should have been disclosed has not been disclosed. And I suppose, therefore, they're asking you to invoke the provisions of Rule 68 bis and use your powers under that Rule to do something. In this particular case, I think they want a report, the Trial Chamber to issue a report. The systematic failure that they focus on in this motion, and in the previous motion, or that they raise in the previous motion, that they highlight at the very least, is that, in their perception or view, the Defence view, there is a problem with investigators alerting the Prosecution team to material that contains disclosable -- that is disclosable. They say that's the systematic failure. The Prosecution submission says that, no, that is not so. The Defence, of course, can have no idea how the Prosecution organises itself, and can have not idea what might or might not cause a failure -- I'm conceding it in this case, I'm not referring to other documents that are the subject of other motions. So the Defence can have no idea how the Prosecution organises itself. And that's illustrated by what I know of the background to this particular document, because in this case, the investigators - in fact, the particular investigator, Mr. Nasir - was scrupulous in bringing it to the attention of the lawyers in the Prosecution team. Your Honour asked me earlier how did this come about, and I am faced with a position of not being able to tell you precisely how it came about, other than the fact that -- well, I can't tell you. It was overlooked, and it may be that the cause of it, again I'm speculating here, it may be that the cause of it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're a very good lawyer, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: The cause of it, if Your Honours please, was the fact that we didn't intend to utilise this person as a witness. I don't know, Your Honour, and I admit from the start that that's my conjecture. But I'm trying to shy away from the fact that it should have been disclosed and it should have been disclosed eight or seven months ago. And I accept that. But to return to my original point: That the Defence focus on a systematic problem is not made out and it is not made out here in this particular case, because you can see that the very fault that they focus on - some problem with investigators - is not the cause of the failure to hand over this particular document as soon as is practicable, within the meaning of Rule 68. So that's what I can say. I wish there was a more specific reason that I could provide to Your Honour as to why it was that it was not disclosed. If there had been, I suppose the problem would have been remedied at a sooner point -- at an earlier point. The Defence also makes clear in its motion to you that the Prosecution -- or submits to you that the Prosecution takes refuge in the issue of prejudice. We're not seeking to take refuge in that issue, because we've admitted our failure to comply with Rule 68. But you cannot say that the question of prejudice is a matter that Your Honours should ignore. And the Appeal Chambers have made that abundantly clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree. You're exempted from pursuing this argument. I agree with you. There is not need to explain it any further. I agree also that it is not part of Rule 68, it's not -- Rule 68 does not depend on whether non-disclosure would cause prejudice or not. But basically whether prejudice has been caused or not is definitely relevant. So you don't need -- MR. DI FAZIO: I accept immediately that the Defence submission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio, if I could kindly ask you either to bring the microphone nearer to you or -- MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry, am I not speaking loudly enough? I do apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or raise your voice a little bit. One of the two. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, the Prosecution accepts the Defence submission that disclosure exists and continues irrespective of whether prejudice is caused. We don't have any quarrel with that whatsoever. But where you have a situation where there has been a breach of the rule, namely, the document not being disclosed as soon as is practicable, the question of what you do brings into play the question of prejudice. The actual prejudice that the Defence will suffer they have identified at paragraph 12 of their submission -- of their motion. They complained that there has been a serious prejudice in the late disclosure of this statement, and they make clear, as Your Honour has already pointed out, that they will have to provide the material in the statement and the report that's part of the statement to their expert. And in particular, they say: "The Defence now has to react in a very short time period, before the Prosecution's military expert, Dr. Arish Turle, testifies, to re-instruct the Defence expert and to receive further comments and opinions from him based on this newly disclosed material." So they've crystallised it. It's made really clear in their motion what the prejudice is, what they're going to suffer, as a result of this late -- eight-month-late disclosure. The Prosecution's submission is that that prejudice simply cannot be so. Dr. Turle is not scheduled to give evidence before Christmas. This case is going -- the Prosecution part of the case is going to go well into the new year. Dr. Turle can be called, and in fact, I believe it had already been the Prosecution's case to call him at a later point in the presentation of its case, and in fact, can be called towards the end of the Prosecution case. We're talking here of not weeks but months, if Your Honours please. Now, surely the Defence can, in a period of months, provide the statement to their expert and say, What do you say about this and let us know your view before we ask any questions of Dr. Turle. So the prejudice that they refer to, in the Prosecution's submission, is either non-existent, or so minor as to be negligible. That, in essence, is the Prosecution's submission. Can I just return to the issue of the more generalised complaint of systematic failure. This statement in itself is a clear example of why there isn't a systematic failure. It's a -- this was a statement that called for disclosure immediately. And it's obvious. It doesn't take long to read to it -- to understand that. I say that because -- and I say that to illustrate the fact that something -- it's purely and simply a question of overlooking the obvious. There's no quarrel on the part of the Prosecution that it should have been disclosed. It's so obvious that it's a mystery to us why it wasn't. So having said that, though, it's not as if -- the point that I'm trying to make is that it's not part of a systematic failure. It stands out. Clearly this should have been disclosed, and there's a lot of material that's very easily discernible as disclosable, and this is and it slipped through the net. And for that the Prosecution apologises. But we ask you to look at the prejudice and say, Well, what's the consequence to the Defence? Surely they can get their expert to comment on the material in that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. Mr. Jones. I am asking you; I don't know who is dealing with this, but I am assume that you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I'll be brief. Just four brief points of reply. As Your Honours have seen, this motion is entitled the first supplement to our Rule 68 motion. All we can do is react to each instance that we discover of non-disclosure and react to that, and there will no doubt be subsequent filings which we will have to make. We don't know precisely what the Prosecution has, so of course we're shooting in the dark, to a certain extent. But we do consider that these failings are indicative of a systematic failure. We hoped that it was a matter of investigators not drawing attention to the lawyers of these statements, because then it seemed to us that it would be a relatively simple matter to say to the investigators, Can you go off and look at other statements you've taken and review them and see if there's more of this material. If the failing is higher up, then that poses more of a problem, in fact, than if it's merely investigators not drawing attention to this material. I would just make this point: That this trial is receiving a lot of publicity in the former Yugoslavia and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Oh, indeed, it is, Your Honour. And as a consequence of that, we have been contacted by people in the former Yugoslavia and have told us, We have given statements to the Prosecutor about -- which touch, for example, on Prosecution witnesses and which, not to put too fine a point on it, has even suggested that some of them are killers. And those are statements which we have not seen. Even aside from those more dramatic examples, we are continually hearing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But, listen, if you have these allegations or this information and you can pinpoint particular cases, then please come forward. I mean, it's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but this is Rule 68 material that the Prosecution has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. But I think what we have at stake at the present moment is the question of whether there has been a systematic failure or not, because this Tribunal is what it is and no one is perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you cannot expect in any given case that the disclosure under either 66 or 68 to be always impeccable, 100 per cent. It does happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It does happen. We step in and we take even drastic steps when it is intentional, when it is in bad faith, when it is systematic. But when it is incidental, one closes a blind eye and moves ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, if you say that you have indications that the Prosecution has failed to disclose to you statements by other persons relative to certain witnesses that have come forward, or may be coming forward, that have not been disclosed to you, then come forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. We'll take a tactical decision on how to deal with that. As far as prejudice is concerned, finally, the response of the Prosecutor puts in mind the essence of someone who would say, Well, I speed a lot but I've never had an accident. Well sooner or later, if you speed continually, there's going to be an accident, and we'll see this afternoon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or you become a Formula 1 racer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We'll see this afternoon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What afternoon? Why are you speaking of the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I was thinking that we were going to deal with the second motion after Ms. Manas concerning the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not sitting in the afternoon, are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, after 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies. Where a witness has come to The Hague, given testimony, and then left, and then we receive a videotape of him giving a statement, as well as others. There is prejudice. The Prosecution says, well, one can simply reinstruct our expert. Well, unfortunately, on the Defence side, it's not that simple. We receive a budget to instruct and expert and to commission a report from him. Once we pay him to do that, we don't have funds to go back to him and say, Here's some more material, can you keep looking at it. It's not that simple. We require timely disclosure so that we can properly prepare for trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's perfectly understandable.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to draw your attention to the aspect of the tactical decision to be taken by the Defence team whether or not to disclose to the Prosecution team the names which are involved -- which are involved in -- specific persons who informed the Defence team that they made statements to the OTP. We really would appreciate to learn about this tactical decision, because we are happy to do an extra check on those specific names to facilitate the disclosure possibilities. And we would like to know what the outcome of the tactical decision is, because if their decision is that they would prefer not to provide us with those names, we would like to note it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your responsibility is there under Rule 68, in any case, Mr. Wubben. I don't think it depends on whether the Defence comes forward and indicates to you the information -- gives you the information or not. I mean, they can wait and use it tactically. You know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if what Mr. Jones is saying is correct, and I have no reason to doubt it, then it's a signal to you to recruit enough resources in your team to do a thorough check and see whether there are any other statements by other individuals relating to some of the witnesses you have in this case - you had an indication also that some of the witnesses may have been killers themselves - and see whether this is another case of another case of unfortunate disclosure and be remedied at this time by prompt disclosure under Rule 68. Beyond that, I'm not going to tell Mr. Jones anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Neither would I. It is a request, and that's why I labeled this as an extra --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it's not a request of the Trial Chamber, it's a request of the Prosecution. Let's make that clear. All right. I think we can -- I think we can close on this matter. We will reserve judgement on it. We still, obviously, have to discuss whether we will give a decision or whether we will leave it pending until the next case of non-disclosure comes up, and then we'll be in a position to see -- to decide whether it is a systematic failure. That, we'll see ourselves and we'll let you know in due course. But it's not something that we are definitely going to decide now, or in the very near future. It probably will be delayed, depending on the outcome of the debate that we will have in camera between the three Judges. Shall we attack the next item on the agenda now, or shall we have a break now? What do you prefer? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I'm in Your Honour's hands. I suppose Mr. Jones is ready to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Better stay away, Mr. Di Fazio, because if you are in my hands, as we go along, you're going to suffer. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I'm happy to go ahead and do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go ahead. MR. DI FAZIO: -- and deal with the video motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we'll start with that. We'll go with the video. Again, I want to make sure that we are not dealing with persons or names who are protected. I don't think we are. MR. DI FAZIO: No, I don't think we are. No, I don't think there are any substantial issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Before we do so, again, I think we owe it to the public, in general, the outsiders, to know exactly what we are talking about, why we are going to see a video not in the course of the testimony --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I mention one matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Apologies for interrupting Your Honour. There may be a technical matter beforehand, which is this video contains interviews with -- well, certainly four people who are of interest to us. I won't mention the names now. One of them is actually interviewed twice, and the second interview, towards the end of the video, is actually, in our submission, the more important interview, and that has not been transcribed by the Prosecution. And so we would certainly want that part of the video also to be played. So it may be a technical matter, because there won't be an English transcript, the interpreters would have to do their best. I think I can mention the names. It's Jovan Nikolic. He's interviewed twice. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I'm grateful for my learned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm grateful to my learned friend for pointing that out, because I wasn't aware of that, I hadn't realised it. I've caused transcripts to be prepared, which obviously must be what I assume is the first segment of his appearance in the videotape. Getting that transcribed and prepared for you so that you can understand the Defence point and the Prosecution reply, we can't do that this morning, and we would have to get a full transcript. So do you want to put off -- do Your Honours want to put off viewing the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think basically we can divide it into two parts. My intention this morning was to deal with this matter only insofar as it relates to witness Eric, and to discuss whether Eric should be brought for an additional cross-examination. And not to discuss the rest, because I don't think it was on our agenda to discuss the rest. That's how I understood it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was our submission, Your Honour, that the other interviews would have been relevant to our cross-examination of Eric, and that's why we were directing Your Honours' attention also to the other interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But we don't need to see those today or to show them to the public today. I mean, the whole point, the whole point is that what needs to be seen today for our own satisfaction is the part of the video where Eric appears, Eric appears, and I'm now going to give information on what your motion is about, and so then everyone can follow. And leave it at that time. And obviously the rest of the video can be used even when Eric is brought -- is summoned again to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, it just strengthens our submission that if we had seen this video, we would have put points on Nikolic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, okay. But it all depends on whether Eric should be brought along or not. I don't think we need to see the rest of the video in public. We can see it in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. That's quite true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for the purpose of informing the public on what is happening: On the 18th of November, 2004, the Defence filed an urgent motion regarding late disclosure of evidence, and to recall a witness -- and to recall a witness. The gist of the motion is the following: Already during the pre-trial conference held on the 28th of September, 2004, the Defence complained that the Prosecution had failed, despite repeated requests to disclose certain video footage on a CD to them. In that context, there appeared at the time to be some misunderstanding as to the contents of the CD in question. You will recall the debate on that occasion. Mr. Di Fazio, from the Prosecution, undertook on that occasion to review the video footage and to resolve the matter. Subsequently, or eventually, the footage in question was disclosed to the Defence on the 10th of November, the 10th of this month. That's eight days before this motion that we are going to debate now was filed. The contention of the Defence is the following: The Defence states that "the video contains highly relevant and extremely important material," I am quoting from the motion. "Regarding events in Kravica," including interviews with several people. The following are mentioned: Slavica Eric, a gentleman who testified in this case on the 26th of October; Ratko Nikolic, who is scheduled to testify in this case on the 3rd of December; and Miladin Bogdanovic, who you know now will not be able to testify because of the medical certificate we have. And Jovan Nikolic, the commander of the Territorial Defence unit of Kravica during the relevant time period. Particularly with regard to Witness Eric, the Defence points out, inter alia, that in the video, Eric is seen wearing a uniform, whereas when he gave evidence on the 26th of October, 2004, he stated that he only wore an old JNA shirt and no uniform. The Defence notes that they would like to cross-examine him on this issue, as well as on other related issues, including the contents of the interviews with the others. Consequently, the Defence seeks an order from this Trial Chamber to have Mr. Eric recalled for further cross-examination. The Defence also points out that the interview with Eric is material which the Prosecution was obliged to search for and disclose before trial, pursuant to Rule 66(A)(ii). Since this is your motion, Ms. Vidovic or Mr. Jones, I give the floor to you first, unless the Prosecution is in agreement with the motion, which would cut short the debate and solve most of the problems. Are you against having Mr. Eric being brought again for further cross-examination? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think for the moment I wouldn't seek to enlarge upon the motion to the extent that I hope it's self-explanatory. I would emphasise the point which I was seeking to make earlier that it's not simply the fact that Mr. Eric is in uniform but the contents of the other interviews which provides material which could have properly been put to him in cross-examination. One other matter is that I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you identify those?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you identify the other points that arise out of the interviews with the other gentlemen that were mentioned that would form part of your additional cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Jovan Nikolic, for one, in his interview, speaks of how 49 of his best soldiers were killed during the -- 49 of his best soldiers were killed during the attack of the 7th of January, 1993, which is an issue going to military necessity and the militarisation of the town, which Mr. Eric was understating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What else?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Understating in his testimony. We also have in the interview of Jovan Nikolic, the second one, I believe it is -- no, it's the first one. He speaks of how the women and children, I believe, Serb women and children were evacuated to Serbia so that the village could be defended essentially by soldiers, again, an issue of evacuation of civilians, which is a matter which we were putting to Mr. Eric. Those points, certainly, we would seek to put to him. If I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With regard to the other gentlemen?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If Your Honour will allow me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Bogdanovic, for example, or Ratko Nikolic, is there anything arising from their interview which prompts you to put additional questions on cross-examination if Mr. Eric is brought over?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Mr. Bogdanovic speaks about trenches in Jezestica; again, a issue which has been put to the witness, the question of defence lines, et cetera. Ratko Nikolic talks about the attack briefly in his interview. Perhaps Ratko Nikolic, the point is rather for his importance -- for his coming testimony. If I may make one separate point. I was thinking that this motion might be considered after the testimony of Ms. Manas. One question which I wanted to put to her is the searchability of these IIFs and MIFS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can always put it to her later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Again, that's a matter which we touch on in our motion, how this error could have occurred, of it being logged and lost, the video, and that's something I would seek to return to possibly after her testimony. But apart from that, I would reserve my right to reply to the Prosecution response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones. Mr. Di Fazio, why are you objecting to Mr. Eric being brought again here for further cross-examination? MR. DI FAZIO: Because if you view the video, there's nothing that is inconsistent with what is depicted in the video with his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why precisely I have asked Mr. Jones -- before seeing the -- watching the video, this is precisely why I have asked Mr. Jones to point out which areas are covered by the various interviews that would prompt the need for a further cross-examination or an additional cross-examination. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On matters that were not touched before or could not have been touched before, or would have been touched before had this video been available at the time. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. If Your Honours please, with respect to the other points raised by Mr. Jones, I can answer with respect to Jovan Nikolic, but only in respect of the first segment, because I haven't seen -- I hadn't realised there was a second segment, and I would need to see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're going to see it now because we're going to see the whole -- how long is this video? MR. DI FAZIO: We can go straight to the points. It's quite a long video, but we can go to the specific parts of the video that show the relevant bits --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we will have a 30-minute break starting from now, during which time, please, someone from your side will identify the various bits and pieces of the video that we'll need to see. I would skip the part relating to Ratko Nikolic, basically, because I don't think we need to -- MR. DI FAZIO: My submission would have been he's coming and they've got the video. So that's the end of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. No, no, but I would suggest that we skip Ratko Nikolic altogether, because -- MR. DI FAZIO: You mean depicting him later in court. Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we'll have a 30-minute break. We'll reconvene at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we are now going to watch the relevant part of this video recording. Does it have an exhibit number already? MR. DI FAZIO: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought so. I thought so. MR. DI FAZIO: It hasn't been tendered into evidence yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we'll have any further submissions you may or may not have, I mean, it depends. But if you have submissions, we'll have those, and that will then adjourn as far as this motion is concerned, and we'll decide it in due course. That's number one. And then I think you will need to decide whether to proceed with the testimony of Ms. Manas, which is not urgent, or not. Our inclination is that if she's not in the position to finish today, that we postpone it until some other day. That's our inclination. MR. DI FAZIO: That's fine by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'd rather not split it into two parts, for various reasons. But I think you've got enough experience to understand precisely what I mean. So I understand that the technicians have been given information as to the various parts that we need to see. MR. DI FAZIO: Certainly. That can be done shortly. Can I just mention one or two matters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Of course, the motion is not just limited to the single issue of the recall. It also goes into the history of this matter, and dare I say it, it raises, for want of a better word, a disclosure-type issue. I want to address you about that because there's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you insisting on that, Mr. Jones, or not? Because more or less you know what our approach is on the matter, and if it can spare us a few minutes, I think that would be to everybody's advantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. For our part, we're content simply to have that on the record in the form of our motion. I can quite understand why Mr. Di Fazio might want would to offer his explanation. That's a matter for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's give the opportunity for Mr. Di Fazio, in any case, to provide an explanation, and then the matter is, for all intents and purposes, left at that, and obviously it goes on record. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. If Your Honours please, the Defence motion makes a generalised complaint of inaction on the part of the Prosecution in respect of this particular portion of evidence. In paragraph 7 of the motion, the Defence submits this: "The matter was further discussed in depth at the Pre-Trial Conference held on the 28th of September, 2004. The matter concluded with Mr. Di Fazio undertaking to review the video material with a view to resolving the impasse. Nothing further was heard from the Prosecution on this matter until the correct video was finally disclosed to the Defence on the 10th of November, 2004." So a generalised complaint of inaction, as I say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He was expecting you to report to him every day. Today I have done this, tomorrow I plan to ... MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. In fact, if Your Honours please, the Defence wrote -- sorry, the Prosecution wrote twice to the Defence on the issue. On the 3rd of October, as part of a long letter dealing with disclosure issues generally, we wrote to the Defence, and at paragraph 9 of that letter -- so, you'll recall, the 28th of September is the start date which our inaction commences, say the Defence, and then the disclosure date which is in November. So on the 3rd of October, we wrote to them: "With respect to the pictorial description of the attack on Kravica, identified as 'Serb TV video review of Muslim attack on Kravica,' I'm satisfied with the CD disclosed to you which contains identical material to the exhibit contained in our exhibit list." In other words, you have the same material that we do. "Mr. Di Fazio is currently reviewing that material, and we shall advise you by Tuesday, the 5th of October, if we intend to make use of the exhibit as part of the Prosecution case." So we addressed the issue on that day. You'll recall that the problem arose of this video because it showed events that you couldn't describe as an attack on Kravica because it was labeled as an attack on Kravica. On the 5th of October, we wrote to the Defence, specifically on that very topic. "We have completed reviewing the above-mentioned item of evidence. I can confirm that, in fact, the item does not depict the attack on Kravica, and was wrongly labeled as such when placed into the evidence collection of the OTP. It depicts a miscellany, miscellaneous items. I can confirm that you have not received the CD that corresponds to the CD in the possession of the Prosecution," using the number, and I don't need to quote it. And I then go on to briefly point out what the video that we had shown them talked about. And then the Prosecution wrote: "In the meantime, every effort will be made to locate any visual depictions of the attack on Kravica in the possession of the OTP, and such material will be disclosed to you as soon as possible." 5th of October. The investigator, whose name has been mentioned this morning, Mr. Nasir, commenced looking for the material, trying to get to the bottom of it, how it was that we had a description of a Kravica attack video, I'll call it that, yet the material we hand over doesn't show that. So in October, late October, he started to go to sources that he thought might solve the mystery. He went to the Netherlands Institute of War Documentation, trying to get a copy of the tape. He contacted them over a period of days. He was eventually informed by that institute that they did not have any such videotape of the Kravica attack. He then turned his attention to a certain individual in the former Yugoslavia who might be able to assist in his investigations, and again, made inquiries lasting several days with that person. That person was also unable to assist in locating the video. Finally, he decided, well, that the best way to try and locate this is to ascertain what the investigator who had -- who was said to have logged, put into the system, so to speak, the tape, what he had -- what else he had put in around that period of time, and he went through it methodically. And he finally came to a video bearing ERN number V000-2774, which, in turn, was wrongly mislabeled. However, he didn't stop there. He kept looking, looked at it and thought this might have been the material, and it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How was it labeled? What was the name given to that video or that item? MR. DI FAZIO: "Videotape of Assault on JNA Convoy in Tuzla." Now, that's how the mistake happened, and it's not -- it's regrettable, but these things happen with the massive documentation. And the Prosecution, rather than leaving the matter alone, did precisely the opposite. We chased it. And if you recall, I can't remember the precise detail, but I know this issue arose at some point, and it might have been during the Pre-Trial Conference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It arose during the Pre-Trial Conference, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: You may recall my emphatic indications to the Trial Chamber that we were, the Prosecution was extremely interested in locating this document, and it was, and it continued looking for it. So the impression that is conveyed to you in the motion of the Defence really provides you with a quite mistaken impression --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I suppose Mr. Jones was not aware of all these humungous efforts made by you and Mr. Nasir and others in trying to dig into this huge larder of goodies that you yourself didn't know what they are, because they were labeled -- wrongly labeled. This is the problem. It's like when you have a big deep-freezer and you put the wrong labels on the wrong things, and you're looking for the right thing and you get the wrong thing, or you never find the right thing. So it's -- I've done it sometimes. MR. DI FAZIO: That's the history of the matter. The Defence were pretty clear and confident in their own mind that something fishy, if I may use that word, was going on here. They claimed that nothing further was heard, and yet it was. They claim in their submission that we didn't apologise to the Defence. They claim that the consequences of this mismanagement are grave, indeed. They claim that the mistake is inexplicable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, don't stretch it too far, because you have, sort of, given quite -- what I would consider a very good justification of what happened. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the other hand, let's admit it. I mean, a tape -- video recording of an event should be labeled in such a way as to reflect the event that was recorded, and not to reflect something else. So at the end of the day, when you come forward and say -- because you kept repeating until the end of the pre-trial stage, sorry, Mr. Jones, sorry, Madam Vidovic, we never had, we don't have a recording which deals with the attack on Kravica. There is no such recording in our records. Yet titles and names do not fall from heaven. If someone gave that video recording that particular title, it must have originated from somewhere. So at that point in time, let's put it like this -- I think I'm reflecting the opinion of Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser, if I'm not, please speak out, that we're fully aware of the justification that you did and of the efforts you made at the end of the day to try and locate this tape if it existed at all, and that you finally managed to do that. But still, I mean, again, this is time and effort spent when it could have been all avoided. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, yes, you're right, Your Honours. You're right, it could have been, and it would have all been avoided if the items of evidence were labeled properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not your fault. It's not the fault of Mr. Wubben, Ms. Sellers, obviously. I'm not trying to blame you. I'm happy that you have cleared the air completely as far as it goes. On the other hand, I mean, why blame Mr. Jones for standing up and asking for a videotape on the attack on Kravica when the message was loud and clear that you must have had a tape on the attack of Kravica somewhere, because otherwise no one would have dreamt of labelling a tape, or a particular tape, as such. I mean, who would have invented that? MR. DI FAZIO: Mr. Jones and the Defence are within their rights, and not only within their rights, but it demonstrates diligence on their part for pursuing the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. I would do exactly the same. MR. DI FAZIO: I have no complaint with that, if Your Honours please, and I don't seek to complain about that. And the Prosecution wanted the material just as much. All I'm concerned about is that is there seemed to be a suspicion on the part of the Defence that there is somehow mala fides at work here. There's something fishy. That's all I'm saying. And I want to emphasise that there just wasn't at any point in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can tell you, Mr. Di Fazio, that if the Trial Chamber had at any moment entertained even the least doubt on your genuineness on all of this or your good faith, we wouldn't be dealing with the matters of alleged non-disclosures the way we have. You can rest assured that we'll hit you and you will never know what hit you before you even know that you have been hit. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. Firstly I apologise if I overlooked an item of correspondence from the Prosecution in suggesting that nothing further was heard. I think at the moment that we received the correct video, it seemed like a red herring that we had had correspondence on the wrong video. In terms of suspicions. There is no allegation of mala fides or anything of that nature. We did simply note in our motion, annex 1, that the IIF description of the material refers to Slavica Eric. So of course we thought that it would not be a difficult matter to have find that material through certain electronic search. That's all I would add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. Perhaps you can bring this matter to a close now. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll be very brief, and then I'll go straight into Vaser Eric and then we can look at the -- sorry, Slavica Eric. And, of course, what I've just told you about the history of the discovery of this tape deals with the 66 point raised by the Defence. Whether or not this video is a previous statement within the meaning of the Rules just doesn't arise, because if it was, assume for the sake of argument that it was, we still couldn't have disclosed it because of the problem that I've just told you about. So that's my submission there. So if we turn now to the substance of the motion. The relief that the Defence seek is a recall of Mr. Eric. The motion in paragraph 8 puts their point very clearly. The Defence submits that he testified that the village guards did not have uniforms on the day of the attack. "To cite but one example, Mr. Eric testified that neither he nor the village guards had uniforms on the day of the attack." If you go to the transcript at page 1192, I can read it out to you very briefly, when he was being examined in chief, he was asked: "Well, as a result of the formation of the unit of the battalion, how did things change in terms of how the village guard functioned? Perhaps a little better but mainly the same. Did you receive more uniforms, for example? Answer: No." Now, he's not saying there -- and that's page 1192, that's the support that they rely upon, that he testified that neither he nor the village guard had had uniforms on the day of the attack. He's not saying that. He's saying that on the day of the formation of the unit of the battalion, I believe that was in November of 2002, according to the transcript, they didn't receive uniforms. He's not saying on the day of the attack, which is a month and a bit later, We had uniforms. He's not saying that. So I can't see how they can draw that conclusion. It's not a fine point, it's not a fine point. Anything could have happened between that time and the 8th of January. I'm not quibbling over minor details. He just simply didn't say it. Now, Your Honour Judge Brydensholt went to the issue, as the Defence quite rightly pointed out, and Mr. Eric made clear his position. He said that they received -- sorry, Mr. Eric said in his testimony that he was wearing a shirt that was part of a former --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: JNA. MR. DI FAZIO: -- JNA uniform. And also he said, at page 1266, that numbers of men in the village guard had parts of uniforms, parts, portions of uniforms. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I hate to interrupt in mid-submission, but I don't see how my learned friend cannot cite the previous part of that exchange: "So was this guard uniformed at the 7th of January?" Answer: No." I don't see how my learned friend has omitted that part which is critical to his submissions. MR. DI FAZIO: I don't deny it. It's there in the transcript, and it's there as part of the motion. It's plain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Di Fazio. But don't you think precisely that things being what they are, that Mr. Eric to this trial, to this courtroom or wherever we'd be sitting, would clear up this matter, and should also throw light on his credibility? MR. DI FAZIO: No. Not on the issues that the Defence say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
