utterances.text: All right. Okay. MR. DI FAZIO: -- would shed light on those issues. And this is the main -- the main point that they make. This is the main point the Defence makes. The Defence position in paragraph 9 is that in the video Mr. Eric is clearly seen to be in uniform. Now, when we see the video, you will be able to draw your own conclusions as to just how accurate that is and just how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to see more than a shirt, actually. That's the important part. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, it is. It is the important part, with respect, and that's the -- and that's what the Defence -- the Prosecution is going to ask you to pay particular attention to. Your Honours also have, I think, the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We better check what we have with you so that we know what we don't have. I have here, and please, Judge Eser and Judge Brydensholt, confirm to me, I have here a transcript of the part dealing with Slavisa Eric, his interview on tape, and then Jovan Nikolic. The first one consists of just one page, the second one of two pages. MR. DI FAZIO: Before I go any further, apparently the Defence have approached the Prosecution and said, Oh, there's a mistake here, there's a mistake in this translation. This was prepared late yesterday, on my instructions, to assist everyone in court with this -- dealing with this submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we have an indication as to what is the alleged, or which is the alleged mistake, so that the attention is drawn of the interpreters as we go along to maybe clear this up for us? Yes, Madam Vidovic, please. Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio, for raising this issue. Yes, Madam Vidovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the part of the transcript referring to Mr. Jovan Nikolic, on page 2 it says that children were sent from Serbia, that's the fifth line from the top. In the original, it says that the weak were sent to Serbia, the weak. That is a much broader term than the term "children," and I ask that this be translated properly, because it's highly relevant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. Anything to submit on this point, in particular, before I refer it to the interpreters for their attention as we go along? MR. DI FAZIO: My point is that this is a working tool, this is not an official translation. I had it done hurriedly yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand that. I'm not criticising it. I understand it. I suppose the only way of approaching it is to point it out to the interpreters. As we approach the end -- towards the end of the interview of Mr. Jovan Nikolic, please pay attention to the original words on the tape and you can then translate them or interpret them to us according to what you believe is the correct interpretation. The contention is that where the written translation says, "because this village, knowing for the enemy, for beasts that surround us, sent its children to Serbia," it should read, according to Madam Vidovic, "sent the weakest or the weaker to Serbia," and not "children to Serbia." Is that correct? MR. DI FAZIO: I don't quibble with that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't quibble with either of you because I don't know what the correct interpretation is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would just ask in terms of these working tools that the first -- the second interview of Jovan Nikolic also be played today, the one that starts at 1.08.17, and that a translation, a draft translation be provided of that part of the interview, because that's the one we say is the most important. MR. DI FAZIO: That's the one that we don't have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, it's not a problem. You're not expected to -- I mean, this is perfectly understandable. The interpreters will indulge us and will try to translate as we go along, if they can. If they can't, then we'll find another solution. MR. DI FAZIO: I just have one last point to make, in my submission of today, before you look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have many points. MR. DI FAZIO: And that's this: If you look at the text of this -- the first one, the first text of Slavisa Eric, it fairly -- it's fairly clear that he's talking about events in the past. There's nothing in there that could -- would lead you to think that he's being interviewed on the day of the attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't have a day for this video recording, no? MR. DI FAZIO: No, I haven't, unfortunately. But if you look at the tenure, the tone, of the document, it's clear that he's talking about events in the past, and some way in the past, in the Prosecution's submission. He talks about it being --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't know whether my learned friend gets that from and whether he's giving evidence. There's nothing indicating a date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll see. If there's nothing indicating a day, that's the only consideration that we can make or take -- MR. DI FAZIO: That's fine. But all I'm saying is that the actual text itself, the actual text, he's talking about events in the past. That would strongly tend to indicate that he's not saying this on the 7th of January. That's my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No comments on our part, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. We'll play -- if we can proceed to the depiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we subdue a little bit the lighting in the room? Because everything is reflected on our monitors here. Yes, when we are in a position to proceed, let's proceed with the running of this video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] During the day, during the 7th of January, we had 38 wounded persons, and because it was winter, and it was not possible to evacuate the injured, we had few vehicles, there was nothing to evacuate them with, and so they kept coming into the outpatient's clinic, and we couldn't empty it in any way because there was no way to evacuate them toward the River Drina, the territory that still hadn't been closed off. They kept promising that helicopters would arrive, that "Niva" vehicles would arrive from Bratunac, but they didn't arrive. I can't remember exactly what time it was, but in the afternoon, man arrived who said that we had to evacuate the wounded quickly because the Turks had already arrived at the entrance to the village. We started slowly -- well, in fact, we didn't have time. We had to speed it up. These people were seriously wounded. All those who are able to walk got up and started off slowly, but four, or rather, five wounded remained who couldn't walk and had to be carried. There was Milojica Bogicevic, born in 1976; his mother Mica, who was wounded in both legs; Zeljko Radovic, also seriously wounded who couldn't walk; and Mladjen Savljevic; and Dragan Radovic, who died somewhere around 1.00. He had heavy internal bleeding, and we couldn't evacuate him in any way. So only four wounded persons were left, and as the last people from the defence of the village came, with their assistance, we would take the wounded people out and send them off in the direction we were retreating in, towards the River Drina. MR. DI FAZIO: As far as the Prosecution is aware, that depicts the portion of the tape that the Defence is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My question is the only one, and the most obvious question that I could make: All we could see of this uniform that you are alleging is a shirt, a camouflage shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, that's not a shirt, that's a jacket. A jacket with another camouflage shirt underneath. And as far as we can tell, he's in full uniform. We can't see his trousers. He's certainly not someone wearing, you know, a camouflage T-shirt and then utterly normal civilian clothes over it. To all appearances, he's every inch a soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We were hoping the other clips should be seen as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we're going to see those as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Moreover, it's not a JNA uniform, in our submission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a camouflage uniform, wherever it comes from. I wouldn't be in a position to distinguish a camouflage uniform coming from JNA from a camouflage uniform coming from anywhere else, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It could be a matter of expert evidence. What is important is the witness said his shirt was of the former JNA, and again that's inconsistent with what we've seen, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed with the next part of the video, starting point 0748.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because we are not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Their barricades, obstacles that is, that they had made while they were in power, they were now replaced with the nefarious way of entering the village, killing people and setting villages on fire. The first victim was Stojan Popovic from the village of Magasici who was killed on May 15 at the door to his house where he was born. Since then, we have been losing our sons, our best heroes, and we have been going through a tragedy that would be very difficult to live through again. On May 24th, an attack was organised, and it was already clear at the time that the objective of the Muslim extremists was to remove such a stronghold out of their way. Burning of villages, Donja Brana, Erkovici, Donji Mratinci, Kicino, et cetera. People were killed in those attacks. One of them was Vujadin, Dolijanovic. Miladin Miladinovic was killed on May 27th. On the 29th of May, the Ustashas organised an attack on Kravica, and at the entrance of the village, there was a heavy battle in which we lost 13 people, including Milutin Milosevic, chief of the public security station, and Golub Djevda, a member of the War Staff at the time. Besides them, 11 more honourable men from our village were killed. In view of the fact that they were always using these nefarious channels, these sly moves during the war, the Ustashas were especially active in setting up ambushes for us on the road from Bratunac to Kravica, because they knew we were dependent on Bratunac, that we had to use that road. On June 1st, 1992, I think that was the most difficult time of all. We lost three good heroes, Raso Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One name is unintelligible; remark by interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] And Miodrag Jokic. At 7.30 in the morning we found them in the village of Glogova when they were coming back from there, because they were there on a private business trip. We buried them and we bid farewell to them, and it was clear to us that this was going to be a difficult fight. But despite Glogova and the road, we were constantly in contact with Milici, going through Mratinjci and over Ravno Buljim in order to get to Milici, because the road towards Konjevic Polje was not open. They set up a number of ambushes there. They were constantly intercepting us, killing us, and so on. During one such occasion Dragan was killed, and Risto Lazic, who was a platoon commander, was killed in an ambush while he was in Vrija. Similar thing happened to Krsmojevic, Miodrag. So their motto was to inflict losses every day, to inflict damage on us every day, to hurt our village. We accepted those losses with great difficulty. Every man knows what that means, because this village, knowing about the enemy, the animals that surrounded us, sent its weak to Serbia and stayed there to defend the village, as much as we could. And if necessary, we were prepared to lay down our lives for our village. The Ustashas weren't satisfied to constantly set up ambushes, and they also began to burn villages. They began to take our villages one by one. And before the invasion by the enemy, this was really a lot. It's hard to pick the words in such a situation, because everything that a person could express can be expressed about something like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we have that second excerpt, and this matter of interpretation/translation has been involved. Unless there are objections, it's taken that we're in the draft translation here. Where we have "children," it should read "weak" and not "children." Mr. Jones would also like to ask to view the next part, the subsequent interview of Mr. Nikolic, Jovan Nikolic, and that is at which --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's at 1:08:17, according to my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Has that been marked? Okay. So could I ask the technicians to go straight to that other part of the video recording, please. MR. DI FAZIO: It's in Sanction, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right, okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] The village of Kravica, located on the road 12 kilometres away from Bratunac between two Muslim villages, was a constant threat, or better to say it was an obstacle, something very difficult for the Muslim extremists to deal with. We made our defence plans and did everything to protect our own people and property to avoid the fate of our ancestors in World War II. The Serbian Democratic Party was established in our village, and this was a party which had the task of organising people to prevent bloodshed and the agony that was to follow. We were the first to take up arms to defend our village and who took the decision to defend the people. And we feel that this is our patriotic duty, and that we are honour-bound to do it. The party had its launching there, and we are proud of this. We are proud because we were aware of what our goal was: To protect our people and to prevent the worst from happening. Unfortunately, our plans were not realised. All those barricades and obstacles that they set up when they were in power, they replaced with surreptitious entries into villages, killing people and burning villages. The first victim in all this was Stojan Popovic, from the village of Magasici, who was killed on the threshold of the supermarket on the 15th of May. From then on we lost our sons, we lost our best heroes, and we suffered a tragedy that is very difficult to deal with. On the 24th of May, an attack was authorised, and it was already clear then that the goal of the Muslim extremists was to remove this stronghold from their path. The villages of Mrkovici, Donji Bratinci [phoen], Kicino, so on and so forth. People were killed in these attacks. One of these was Vujadin Dolijanovic. On the 27th of May, Miladin Miladinovic was killed. On the 29th of May, the Ustashas organised an attack on Kravica, and at the entrance to the village, a difficult battle took place in which we lost 13 people, along them Milutin Milosevic, chief of the public security station, and Djevda Golub, a member of the War Staff at the time. Apart from them, 11 other honourable men from our village were killed. With regard to the fact that they always used these nefarious perfidious channels, the Ustashas were especially active in setting ambushes for us on the communication between Bratunac and Kravica because they knew that we had to use this communication towards Bratunac. On the 1st of June, 1992, I think this was the hardest fight at the time, we lost three good heros, Raso Milosevic, Mico - the name was unintelligible - and Miodrag Jokic. We found them in the village of Glogova when they were returning at 7.30 in the morning from a private business trip. We buried them with dignity, we bid farewell to them, and it was clear to us that this fight was going to be a very hard one. Despite Glogova, we had a constant obligation to have contacts with Milici, crossing over Mratinjci and Ravno Buljim in order to get to Milici, because the communication towards Konjevic Polje had not been established. Over there, they set us a number of ambushes. There were constant interceptions, constant killings, and so on. Dragan Satinovic [phoen] was killed during one such contact, and Risto Lazic, who was a platoon commander, was killed in an ambush while he was in Vrija. And Miodrag Krsmojevic suffered a similar fate. Their motto was to inflict losses on us daily, to hurt us daily, to hurt our village. And these losses were something that was very hard for us. Every man means a lot. And what this village meant for the enemies, the beasts surrounding us, we knew this so we sent the weak to Serbia and stayed behind to defend our village, as much as was possible, even if we had to be brave and give our lives for our village. The Ustashas were not satisfied with the ambushes alone. They started organising torchings and burnings of our village. And it is hard to choose words in these situations, because it is necessary to express our anger in the severest words possible. They burnt everything, killed the feeble, women. And when the Ustashas organised an attack on Magasici while the fighters were defending the village, they entered the village perfidiously from the other side and killed a number of children.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot catch all the names.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] In this attack defending the villages, fighters were killed such as- unintelligible - from Jezestica and another man from Jezestica. The descendants of these Ustashas from Jamnjeci [phoen] and Cizmici organised an attack on the village of Jezestica, burning the village and killing ten heroes, including two brothers called Milanovic, Andjelko and Dragan, their mother, Sava. And a hero who arrived from Belgrade defended the village of Osojnica, and they would carry trophies off to Srebrenica to show to each other what they could do. The village of Zivkovica was a constant target for the Ustasha attacks, and it always fended off these attacks with losses. On the 8th of August, when the village of Jezestica was burned down, two good heroes were killed, Jovo Milanovic and Bozo Martic. As of August, until October or December, we lost men daily. Every day we buried our nearest and dearest, said farewell to them, hoping that we will be able to save our village. We cared a lot about our village. We had a village that had everything, a school, a clinic, a church, a coffee shop, a football club, a post office, everything. We cared about our village. We lived for it, and we thought that we could save it. However, losing men, the number of killed and wounded increased daily, and the circle around our village tightened. This happened on the 17th of December. During a strong Ustasha attack, we lost Rajko Tomic, Bato Tadic, and Vasilj Kotadorovic [phoen]. On the 24th, Ustashas enters Glogova, surrounded the village, and then we lost honourable fighters, such as Stanko --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last name.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Minja Jovanovic, Vlajko Janic and Boro Obradovic. After entering Glogova, the village was surrounded, and from day to day we expected what would happen on the bloody Christmas of 1993. Christmas arrived the day when a proud Serbian village was wiped off the face of the earth, the village of Kravica. It disappeared in the Ustasha onslaught, losing 49 of its best fighters; 38 were wounded, and for two and a half months, we could not go back to bury their bones, to give them a decent burial and thank them for everything they have done for us. This is the wartime story of the inhabitants of a village which will rise again probably one day, because our goal has been realised, we have now created the state that we fought for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that all? All right. Any further submissions, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We do have the -- one moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me make -- while you discuss with Madam Vidovic, let me make something very clear: The fact that we have seen these two persons, both Mr. Eric and Mr. Nikolic, here make statements in the form of a TV interview does not qualify these statements as evidence in this case, all right? So I'm making it clear so that later on, there will be no questions on this matter. This is not Mr. Jovan Nikolic testifying in this case, nor is it an additional evidence testimony on the part of Mr. Eric. So I'm making things clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I'm obliged for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I might just make the following observations: This is Jovan Nikolic, the head of the Kravica TO, giving a great deal of information, albeit we say in an extremely one-sided way, speaking about the enemy, referring to Ustasha and Muslim extremists, and so what we say a presentation very much covered by Serb propaganda, but nonetheless revealing a great deal about the tactical situation in the area. And just by way of checklist, I can refer to the fact that he referred to Kravica as a stronghold from quite early on in 1992, that he referred to heavy battles, he referred to a war staff, he referred to actions in Glogova, he referred to difficult fights, he referred to contact with Milici, platoon commanders, nothing on village guards, but everything coloured in military terms, the evacuation of women and children, the establishment of the SDS, about which we've heard from Dr. Gow, in the village, and that it was organising people, that Kravica was the first to take up arms to defend their village, that the SDS was launched in Kravica. He refers to barricades and obstacles, Ustashas throughout, again, we say strong anti-Muslim propaganda. He refers to members of the War Staff, the significance, the strategic significance of the road from Kravica to Bratunac. Of fights leading up to the 7th of January throughout December, and that they were expecting an attack on the 7th of January. All of this, we say -- and also the attack on Jezestica coming from Jaglici and Cizmici. There's reference to volunteers from Belgrade. We say all of this goes to issues of military necessity, which are key on the Kravica charges, and all of which is material which we could properly have put to Slavisa Eric, in the context of this motion, if it had been promptly disclosed. And I referred also, of course, to the fact that 49 of the best fighters died on the 7th of January, indicating a clear military situation and a battle on that day. So it's in that context that I make those submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, many of the topics raised by Mr. Jones were covered by the content of the examination-in-chief. I'm informed by my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's not saying that they weren't. He's saying they would have been covered differently or additionally had he been made aware of the contents of this video at the time. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, that may be so. How would he have been able to approach it? He would have been able to show the witness, Mr. Eric, this particular CD, and then asked him, Do you agree or do you disagree with that, or do you have any information on this particular point that Mr. Nikolic talks about in the course of the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we would have let him do that. MR. DI FAZIO: Then how else could he have used it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But at least he would have had the information. MR. DI FAZIO: But he may have had the information, but, Your Honours, see, the problem is, what the Defence have to do is demonstrate to you, that having had the information -- not having had the information, they were therefore deprived of a particular line of cross-examination. Now, if Your Honours are saying, well, you may not have even allowed him to do that, then they're left in the same position, whether they had the video or not. It's not quibbling, if Your Honours please, because it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I won't comment, because eventually we will have to take a decision on this, and we haven't discussed this amongst ourselves as yet because we haven't seen the video. So I will reserve. Yes, Judge Brydensholt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Do you think it would be possible to determine at what date this video is made? Do you know from where it originates?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in addition to that, don't you think that the return of Mr. Eric would help us at least in regard to the dating of the part in which he appears? Because it doesn't mean to say that Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Eric and Mr. Bogdanovic, and Mr., whoever it is, the other one, were all interviewed on the same day. But at least we will know from Mr. Eric when he was interviewed. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, the attitude of the Prosecution in this case has to be a delicate one. We don't want to stand in the way of Mr. Eric being returned to -- and thereby deprive the Defence of rightful points of cross-examination or deprive the Trial Chamber of rightful inquiries that it may wish to make. The issue that you raise -- that Your Honour Judge Brydensholt raises regarding the timing of the -- of the film footage that we see, I suppose, could be answered by Mr. Eric. You could say, Yes, it was taken three months later, six months later, or taken on the very day. I don't know. But there is every indication that there are other events depicted in the tape that make it -- that certainly could, long after the 7th of January. But to return to my point, all the Prosecution wants to do is to call upon the Defence to provide you with clear, compelling reasons why this man should be returned. If the Trial Chamber takes the view that there are such compelling reasons, then we don't want to stand in the way of justice, and we are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not taking that stand now, obviously. We need to discuss -- MR. DI FAZIO: It's just that if we think about it in practical terms, you've got Mr. Eric back here, he's sitting in the box, what is going to happen? What can the Defence do? They can ask him about the shirt. Well, that is really neither here nor there, because he's got the -- we know what his evidence is. He said he had a JNA uniform on the day. And that it's really -- the issue is relating to Mr. Jovan Nikolic and the various factual matters that he raises that they have to rely upon. I haven't had a chance of analysing all of the transcript of Mr. Jovan Nikolic in minute detail, and you'll remember -- sorry, Mr. Slavisa Eric, in minute detail, and I wasn't the counsel who took him. So if you would like more detailed submissions on each of the points that have been raised by the Defence, I can address you. But the general thrust of the Prosecution's submission is that, as far as the Jovan Nikolic segment is concerned, what would they be able to do? He's talking about a big sweep of events, covering lots of events, a long time. And all they could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is Jovan Nikolic an intended witness or not? MR. DI FAZIO: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But doesn't that strengthen even further the case of the Defence, the argument of the case? MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry, in what respect, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't intend to bring forward Mr. Jovan Nikolic, if he's still available, because I wouldn't even know that. MR. DI FAZIO: Then the Defence will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The only information they can get out of Jovan Nikolic is what they can extract from this interview, which then can -- they can then use not in relation to Nikolic himself, because you are not bringing him forward, but in relation at least to other witnesses. MR. DI FAZIO: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They can definitely use that with other witnesses that you will be bringing forward. MR. DI FAZIO: That's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But obviously they did not have the opportunity to use that material with Slavisa Eric. I'm just arguing with you at the moment, you know, arguing the point with you, not deciding it. MR. DI FAZIO: That's fine. In that case, if Your Honours might then take -- adopt this approach: You might call upon the Defence and say, Okay, you've heard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Call Jovan Nikolic yourself, sort of. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Yes. But they might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think they will rush -- they will ask for an early adjournment of the case so that they file the necessary subpoena, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: You could ask the Defence to say, Okay, what particular piece of information can you see that is depicted in those two segments that you -- that is a revelation to you that you didn't have that you couldn't put to Mr. Eric; and having obtained that, what would have been your course of action? Would you have shown the video to him and then asked Mr. Eric to comment upon it? What if Mr. Eric says, Well, I know nothing about this. Jovan Nikolic can talk until the cows come home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're speculating here. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, this is so. Yes, we are. But the application is to bring this man back. Now, as I said, if the Defence can demonstrate clear, compelling reasons why he should be brought back, the Prosecution will withdraw its opposition. But at this stage, we're not satisfied that such reasons have been demonstrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I add one brief observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you do so, Judge Eser -- okay, all right. Mr. Jones, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's simply --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, simply to say this: Short of going back over our cross-examination and saying for each question how we would have worded it differently, which is obviously micromanagement at the level which I think is not required of us, I would simply make this point, that Jovan Nikolic refers to a lot of actions on different dates, a lot of wounded people. We know that Mr. Eric was an ambulance driver, he was a medical orderly. He certainly should have had knowledge that those fights were going on on those dates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's something -- not necessarily. It's a question of putting points to him. We don't say expect that he would agree with every point we put to him. But it's ammunition we properly should have had in our possession, and I make no more of it than that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: My question may be considered as addressed to both parties. Am I correct in assuming that there are two different issues involved here: The question whether Eric wore a uniform on a certain date, point 1; and what the other contents of his interview would be, giving light with regard to the events on the 7th of January? Is it correct to assume that these are two different issues? MR. DI FAZIO: In one sense --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel please slow down. MR. DI FAZIO: -- Defence submission, no. There are two reasons as to why we bring this man back, why we bring Mr. Eric back. That's the central application. And the reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: That's not my point at this moment. I just wanted to know whether there are two issues involved, wearing a uniform on the 17th of -- 7th of January, on the one side, and additional facts reported upon by Eric in his interview. MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, I see. Well, as I understand it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I think there are two different issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honours are correct. There are two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely. MR. DI FAZIO: That's how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, if I may continue. So far, even if you do not know at this moment at what time the interviews have been taken, it seems quite clear that they would not have been taken on the 7th of January. Is that correct, my assumption? MR. DI FAZIO: That will certainly be the Prosecution position. Every indication that we have from the content of the tape is that it's -- they are interviews that were taken after, after that date. Yes, the use of the language itself, I've already made that point. And in addition, my colleague pointed out that it depicts -- it depicts a funeral in March, held in March 1993. So you would think that it's subsequent to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But if --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just a moment. If March 1993 would have been the time of taking the interview, that would mean that the interviews with Eric on the one side and Nikolic on the other side have not been taken at the same time. MR. DI FAZIO: We don't know that. We simply don't know that, if Your Honours please. And if Mr. Jones is going to say, Well, you just don't know when the interviews or segments were recorded, well, that point is made. All we can do is point to indicia, to indications, for our view that it's footage taken after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: So if we assume that the footage was taken after the 7th of January -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: -- Yes? Now, what would it -- I would like to ask you if my recollection is correct: Eric was saying that he may not have had the uniform on the 7th of January, but that later on he had a uniform. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I believe -- Ms. Sellers may be able to give you more detail on that, and she'll correct me if I'm wrong, but I understand that Eric's testimony was that he later joined the army, and later they got -- and that later they got uniforms. That's my recollection of the testimony, as I read it last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: So I think it would be very material to find out at what time the interview was taken, and whether at that time Eric was already a member of the army, or some army or some uniformed Territorial Defence unit. Is that correct? MR. DI FAZIO: It would be very material if, in fact, he was wearing a uniform and was a member of the army at a later point in time when the film was taken, yes, because then, of course, it doesn't undermine his evidence that he was wearing a shirt on the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we shouldn't concentrate our efforts much on the question of the uniform more than on the rest, because basically I think it would be a waste of the Tribunal's resources to bring Mr. Eric here to tell us -- give us an explanation why on the footage he's wearing an army camouflage jacket and why on the 7th he was wearing a shirt of -- a JNA shirt. But that, again, ultimately we will need to decide that. But the rest is more important than the question on the uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I respond ever so briefly as to the timing. Obviously, the interview has to be after the attack. It's not a prediction of the attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's after the attack. Whether it's that afternoon, whether it's the next day, none of us know. That's the starting point. And we would be comfortable with the Bench drawing assumptions which are the least favourable to the accused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will not draw assumptions. If we don't know, we don't know. It's no use trying to draw assumptions, at least none of us, having been professional judges in our countries, we don't draw assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just want to avoid a construction where we arrive at the conclusion that it must have been many months afterwards when the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, we are technocrats, Mr. Jones, like you are. We don't take -- in a criminal procedure, you don't assume, you prove. You either prove or you don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think we can close the argument on this. We will be deciding this matter -- we will discuss it immediately after the -- in the break, and we will hand down a decision early next week on this. I don't think it presents us with major difficulties. The last thing. I don't recommend that we start with Manas, because we are not going to finish her, and I would rather prefer to use the remaining time to discuss what -- in camera what we have discussed, what we have debated in the courtroom. Yes, Mr. Wubben. I thought you were --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought you were requesting the floor. All right. There are two things that I would like to mention. May I remind you that the next sitting will be on Tuesday; you know that. Also, for your information, the date of the Plenary, which was planned for the 6th of January -- 6th of December, sorry, has now been moved to the 8th of December. So I'm informing you of this now, in case you didn't know, so that you will make the necessary adjustments, because when I was given the list of the witnesses we are to expect between now and mid-December, first there was an indication that you had a witness in line for the 6th, which would have been a problem in any case, because on the 6th we were going to have the Plenary. Now we are not going to have the Plenary on the 6th, so you can retain that witness on the 6th, but you definitely need to shift the witness or witnesses you had planned for -- to come over and testify on the 8th, because on the 8th we will have a full day of Plenary for sure, possibly also to be followed the day after. But that would not create a problem. I mean, I can find a solution for that. But on the 8th, definitely there will not be a sitting, because it's an important -- we are discussing very important matters in Plenary, and I need to be there for more than one reason, one of which is because I chair the Rules Committee. So I won't be able to hold a sitting, and at the same time, be in Plenary. And Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser will need to be present as well at this Plenary, so it's not a question of -- there's no solution to it. We won't sit on the 8th. But you need to shift the order of witnesses. That's it. I don't think there's anything else to discuss --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just apart from our request for a revised witness list, so we can prepare for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It's up to the Prosecution. I'm pretty sure they will provide us with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're working on that list, and we will provide it on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And I take it that on Tuesday we'll sit in the afternoon, not in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that the entire week is in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I remember well. I may be mistaken. It is entirely -- and I don't think there is a way of changing it, because I asked my secretary to see if we could change the dates, but it's difficult -- change the sitting from afternoon to morning, but it's not possible. If it is at all possible, registrar, please let me know, with the exception of Thursday. Thursday I need the morning for myself. So have a nice weekend, all of you, and please, God willing, we'll reconvene on Tuesday, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
